title: How do we change millimetres into centimetres?
description: Lengths in millimetres are written in centimetres by moving the point one place left, and one length is changed back into millimetres. Keeko's doubt is that the point moves two places.
teaching_notes: One idea: a millimetre is one tenth of a centimetre, so the point moves one place. Watch for students who move the point two places because they think of centimetres and metres.

source: Fill in the blanks (mm to cm): 12 mm, 56 mm, 70 mm, 9 mm, 134 mm, and the length in mm that is 203.6 cm.
video_script.why: The child has written fractions as decimals and now uses them to change one unit of length into another.
video_script.substitution: One millimetre is one tenth of a centimetre, so the point moves one place when the unit changes.
video_script.anchor: a ruler with one centimetre cut into ten millimetres
video_script.wrong_move: moves the point two places, as for centimetres and metres
video_script.payoff_line: Millimetres to centimetres moves the point one place left

final_answer.spoken: five point six, seven point zero, zero point nine and thirteen point four centimetres; and two thousand thirty-six millimetres

maths_rules: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 mm = 1/10 cm = 0.1 cm
12 mm = 10 mm + 2 mm = 1 cm + 0.2 cm = 1.2 cm
the slip: 0.09 cm would be 9/100 cm, but 9 mm is 9/10 cm
video_script.design: The ruler stays on the stage with one centimetre cut into ten millimetres; each length slides to its place in the working band and the point moves one place. Keeko's doubt moves the point twice.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book, then a ruler marked in cm and mm; lengths 12 mm, 56 mm, 70 mm, 9 mm, 134 mm and 203.6 cm; a question mark in the anchor band

marks.list: the lengths are written beside the ruler

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about changing millimetres into centimetres.
<bookmark mark='list'/>Lengths such as twelve millimetres, fifty-six millimetres and nine millimetres are to be written in centimetres.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>One length goes the other way, two hundred three point six centimetres in millimetres.

beats.on_screen: the lengths stay on the board; Keeko sits beside them as the child
narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a ruler: one centimetre cut into 10 equal millimetres; one millimetre marked as 1/10 cm = 0.1 cm

marks.ruler: the ruler is drawn with one centimetre cut into ten parts
marks.tenth: one millimetre is marked as 0.1 cm

narration: <bookmark mark='ruler'/>Look at a ruler. One centimetre is cut into ten equal parts, and each part is one millimetre.
<bookmark mark='tenth'/>A millimetre is one tenth of a centimetre, which is zero point one centimetre.

beats.on_screen: Given: 12 mm, 56 mm, 70 mm, 9 mm, 134 mm and 203.6 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, twelve, fifty-six, seventy, nine and one hundred thirty-four millimetres.
Also two hundred three point six centimetres.

beats.on_screen: To find: the millimetre lengths in centimetres, and the last length in millimetres
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write the millimetres in centimetres, and the last length in millimetres.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 1 mm = 1/10 cm = 0.1 cm; 12 mm = 10 mm + 2 mm = 1 cm + 0.2 cm = 1.2 cm

marks.twelve: 12 mm is split into 10 mm and 2 mm

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step one, one millimetre is one tenth of a centimetre, which is zero point one centimetre.
<bookmark mark='twelve'/>Twelve millimetres is ten millimetres plus two millimetres, which is one centimetre plus zero point two centimetres.
<bookmark mark='join'/>That is one point two centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 56 mm = 5.6 cm; 70 mm = 7.0 cm; 9 mm = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = 13.4 cm; the point moves one place left

marks.move: an arrow shows the point moving one place left

narration: <bookmark mark='move'/>Step two, each millimetre is a tenth, so the point moves one place to the left.
<bookmark mark='fifty'/>Fifty-six millimetres is five point six centimetres, and seventy millimetres is seven point zero centimetres.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>Nine millimetres is zero point nine centimetres, and one hundred thirty-four millimetres is thirteen point four centimetres.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 203.6 cm x 10 = 2036 mm; the point moves one place right

marks.back: an arrow shows the other way
marks.mult: 203.6 x 10 is written with the point moving one place right

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step three, go the other way for two hundred three point six centimetres.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Each centimetre is ten millimetres, so we multiply by ten and the point moves one place right.
<bookmark mark='two'/>That gives two thousand thirty-six millimetres.

marks.l1: the four centimetre lengths are marked

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Millimetres to centimetres moves the point one place left.
<bookmark mark='l1'/>The lengths are five point six, seven point zero, zero point nine and thirteen point four centimetres.
<bookmark mark='l2'/>Two hundred three point six centimetres is two thousand thirty-six millimetres.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the ruler
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 9 mm = 0.09 cm appears and is struck out; the ruler shows 9 of the 10 parts of one centimetre; 0.9 cm is written

marks.fix: 0.09 is struck out and 9 of the 10 parts are shaded

beats.removed: the second move of the point
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks nine millimetres is zero point zero nine centimetres, because the point moves two places.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But a centimetre is only ten millimetres, not a hundred. The point moves one place, and nine millimetres is zero point nine centimetres.
